extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, playwrights, critics, and comedy writers studying theory of humour
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical analysis of comic mechanisms in situations and language: identifies modes (repetition, inversion, interference, transposition) that produce laughter and shows how to apply them to words, scenes and wit. Useful for critics, dramatists and writers seeking principled methods for producing or analysing humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy arises from repetition: characters / actions represent constant forces that combine the same way, so the same situation is reproduced; repetition makes a scene a classical type or model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat a set of actions or relations 'as it is' or transfer them bodily to another set with partial resemblance — this mechanises life and produces the comic. Example: stock classical scenes become amusing 'de facto' by partial resemblance to an established comic model. Note: repetition is likened to the 'favourite' device of light comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (role reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse the situation and invert the rôles to obtain a comic scene (topsyturvydom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inversion can be shown directly (both scenes played) or indirectly (one scene shown while the other exists in the audience's mind). Examples: a prisoner lecturing the magistrate, a child presuming to teach parents, the villain who becomes victim of his own villainy, 'robber robbed'. Inversion is less powerful in the verbal plane but widely used by professional wits (e.g., subject/object reversal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of independent series
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation is comic when it belongs simultaneously to two altogether independent series of events and can be interpreted in two entirely different meanings at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad phenomenon includes equivocal situations and stage-made misunderstandings. Laughter comes from revealing the coincidence of the two independent series and the continual threat of their 'dissolving partnership' being patched up again. Examples: juxtaposing past/present series (Bonivard + Tartarin manacled together), mock-heroic transpositions, building two comedies within one play so they intermittently interfere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivocal situation / stage-made misunderstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular instance of reciprocal interference where actors know only one aspect while the public sees the real meaning, producing oscillation between possible and real meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author must show every aspect to the audience and constantly recall the double fact of independence-and-coincidence (renewing the threat of collapse) so the misunderstanding serves as a sign of interference. The misunderstanding itself is not laughable except as signal of the interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life / absentmindedness (comic in events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective of light comedy is to obtain a 'mechanisation of life' — treating life as a repeating, reversible mechanism; the ludicrous in events is 'absentmindedness in things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerate naturally occurring rigidity/absentmindedness into a system or art (jointed dancing-doll analogy). Light comedy depends on a previously-accepted convention; its link to real life is fragile. Because absentmindedness in events is exceptional and slight, comedy amplifies it for pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in words (language-as-source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between comic expressed via language (translatable) and comic created by language (owing to sentence structure or word choice) — the latter often cannot be translated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language itself becomes comic by lapses of attention within language (rigidity, ready-made formulas, figurative/literal plays). Analyse how the methods used for actions/situations (repetition, inversion, interference) project onto the plane of words to obtain all possible forms of comic speech and wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between comic and witty (esprit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is 'comic' when it makes us laugh at the person who utters it; 'witty' when it makes us laugh at a third party or at ourselves. There is often ambiguity, and witty remarks correspond to fleeting comic scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit may be seen as the comic in a highly volatile (fugitive) state. To analyse wit, expand the remark into a full scene and identify its comic category. Witty thinking is 'dramatic' — ideas converse like persons and are staged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to analyse witty remark (enlarge into scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical procedure: take the witty remark, enlarge it into a regular scene, then identify the comic category it belongs to to reduce the remark to its simplest elements and fully explain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mme. de Sévigne's 'Your chest hurts me' becomes a Molière scene (doctor feeling father's pulse and diagnosing the daughter). This shows how a witty quip corresponds to a comic situation (jointed-doll / sympathy literalisation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / ready-made phrase + absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic meaning is invariably obtained when an absurd idea is fitted into a well-established phrase-form that signals automatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language contains stereotyped phrase-endings; inserting a palpable error or contradiction into such a formula reveals the speaker's automatism and becomes comic. Examples: M. Prudhomme's 'Ce sabre est le plus beau jour de ma vie' (mixing disparate phrase-forms), 'I don't like working between meals' (plays on hygiene proverb). Such comic sayings often survive translation poorly because the phrase-form is language-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking figurative expressions literally (materialising metaphors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect is obtained whenever we pretend to take literally an expression that was used figuratively — divert attention to the physical when the moral is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most words have a concrete (material) and a moral (figurative) meaning; forcing attention onto the material aspect of a metaphor makes it laughable. Examples: 'Tous les arts sont frères' → changing gender 'sœurs' produces comic effect; sporting metaphors turned into literal races yield wit (Boufflers 'I'll back the joke!').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference / play upon words and puns
rubrics_metrics.description: The reciprocal interference of two sets of ideas inside one sentence is a rich comic source: from the crude pun (two different sentences sounding the same) to a true play upon words where one sentence legitimately carries two independent meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pun is the least reputable form; true word-play exploits multiple meanings of a word (literal vs figurative) to reveal a negligence or lapse of attention in language. This is analogous to stage reciprocal interference and produces amusement by making language momentarily forget its normal function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion and transposition of sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal inversion (reversing sentence elements, e.g., subject/object) and transposition (placing an idea in another 'key') produce comic meanings when the sentence still makes sense or yields two readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inversion is easy and common among professional wits (e.g., 'What do you mean by emptying your pipe on my terrace?' → 'What do you mean by putting your terrace under my pipe?'). Transposition is likened to repetition in action and is described as even more far-reaching: a phrase reversed but still meaningful or expressing two independent sets of ideas is likely to be comic.
